subject: English
passage:
Text 1
Documentary films are gaining recognition in academic circles, but they shouldn't be classified as literature. By definition, literature creates meaning through written narrative structure only; documentary films convey their messages primarily through visual footage and use written elements only minimally, in subtitles and credits. Documentary films are experienced as moving images and not as written narrative, making them more similar to journalism than to literature.

Text 2
Documentary films present their arguments through both written elements and visual footage. Without narration scripts and title cards, viewers would be unable to understand the significance of what is shown in the footage: the meaning emerges from the integration of text and image. Moreover, Errol Morris's The Fog of War and many other documentary films feature narration that is as eloquently crafted as the prose found in many acclaimed novels. Therefore, documentary films qualify as literary works.
prompt: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the overall argument presented in Text 1?

choices.A: By acknowledging that the author of Text 1 has identified a weakness that is common to all documentary films
choices.B: By asserting that written narrative plays a more important role in documentary films than the author of Text 1 recognizes
choices.C: By suggesting that the themes of certain documentary films are more complex than the author of Text 1 claims
choices.D: By agreeing with the author of Text 1 that most documentary films aren't as sophisticated as most literary works are

explanation:
Choice B is the best answer because it most accurately states how the author of Text 2 would most likely respond to the argument presented in Text 1. In arguing that documentary films shouldn't be classified as literature and are more comparable to journalism, Text 1 claims that written narrative plays a relatively limited role in documentary films: visual footage, not written elements, is the primary means by which documentary films convey their messages, and written elements are used "only minimally"—that is, comparatively very little—in the form of subtitles and credits. However, the author of Text 2 asserts that written elements in documentary films are as equally vital for creating meaning as visual footage, since without narration scripts and title cards, viewers wouldn't be able to understand the significance of what they're seeing. Moreover, the author of Text 2 argues that there are many documentary films that feature "eloquently crafted" narration whose written quality is as accomplished as any acclaimed novel. Because Text 1 argues that written narrative is subordinate to visual footage in documentary films, whereas Text 2 highlights how written elements are an essential component of a documentary's meaning-making, it can reasonably be inferred that the author of Text 2 would say that written narrative plays a more important role in documentary films than the author of Text 1 recognizes.

Why A is incorrect:

Choice A is incorrect. Although Text 1 indicates that documentary films shouldn't be classified as literature based on their minimal use of written elements, there's no indication that the author of Text 1 considers this minimal use as a weakness, just that it doesn't fit the particular definition of "literature" proposed in the text. Even if Text 1 had suggested that their use of written elements was a common weakness of documentary films, the author of Text 2 emphasizes how many documentary films feature "eloquently crafted" narration, and would therefore say that their written elements are exemplary, not that they are weak.
